title: Libraries, Modules, Imports, and Dependency Concepts
learningObjectives: Describe the purpose of this function-related concept.
Identify its key parts or rules in an example.
Trace a simple execution or information flow.
Explain a common misuse and how to avoid it.
Apply the concept to a small programming task.

understand.concept: A library is reusable code provided for a particular purpose. A module is an organizational unit that may define and expose code or data. Importing or requiring a module makes selected capabilities available to another part of a program. Dependencies are code or resources a project relies on; they may be built-in, local, or external and should be managed deliberately.
understand.whyItMatters: Libraries and modules avoid reimplementing common capabilities and help establish boundaries. External dependencies also introduce version, maintenance, security, licensing, and compatibility considerations.
understand.analogy: A workshop borrows a tool from a shared tool cabinet instead of building every tool itself. The analogy does not describe package versioning, dependency resolution, or code execution risks.
understand.analogyLimit: This analogy omits language-specific implementation details; use it only as a first mental model.

explain.narrative: Check what a library offers, how it is imported, and which names it exposes. Prefer documented, necessary dependencies. Review versions and sources, and avoid adding a package simply because it is convenient when a built-in feature or small local function is sufficient.

examples.title: Use a built-in library concept
examples.code:
// JavaScript example using a built-in Math capability
console.log(Math.max(3, 8, 5));
examples.explanation: The language runtime supplies Math; no third-party package is needed.

examples.title: Import a named capability
examples.explanation: The importer uses a name that the module exports; the exact file must exist.

examples.title: Default import concept
examples.explanation: A default export is imported using the module's default-export convention.

examples.title: Dependency inventory
examples.explanation: Listing a dependency is not proof that it is safe; source and version still need review.

examples.title: Avoid unnecessary package
examples.code:
function clamp(n, low, high) { return Math.min(Math.max(n, low), high); }
console.log(clamp(14, 0, 10));
examples.explanation: A tiny local helper may be simpler than adding an external dependency.

commonMistakes: Splitting code into too many tiny pieces or overly broad components.
Ignoring inputs, outputs, or assumptions at boundaries.
Assuming runtime behavior is identical across languages.
Using abstraction or dependencies without a clear benefit.
